content: Obesity is a significant public health issue in modern society. The intragastric balloon (IGB) has been developed as a temporary intervention to assist in the management of obesity. Its primary purpose is to aid individuals who have not achieved satisfactory results through clinical obesity treatments, even when managed by a multidisciplinary team. It is also considered for patients with severe obesity who face higher risks associated with surgical interventions. However, the comparative effectiveness of different IGB procedures, both against conventional treatments and among themselves, remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of the intragastric balloon in individuals with obesity. To gather relevant studies, comprehensive searches were conducted across multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and The Cochrane Library. Additional efforts included reviewing reference lists of pertinent articles, manually searching selected journals, and consulting experts in the field. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that met specific inclusion criteria. Given that short-term weight loss is common, only studies reporting outcomes after a minimum follow-up period of four weeks were considered. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and independently verified by two others. The quality of the trials was also independently assessed by two reviewers. A total of nine randomized controlled trials involving 395 participants were included in the analysis. Six of these studies had follow-up periods of less than one year, with the longest study lasting 24 months. Only one-third of the included studies demonstrated a low risk of bias. Importantly, no data were available regarding quality of life, all-cause mortality, or morbidity. When compared to conventional obesity management, the IGB did not provide compelling evidence of superior weight loss outcomes. However, complications associated with IGB placement were observed, though most were minor in nature. The risk of minor complications, such as gastric ulcers and erosions, was significantly increased. The authors concluded that the evidence from this review is insufficient to guide definitive decision-making due to the substantial variability in the methodologies and clinical aspects of the included IGB trials. Some authors noted that the motivation and encouragement to adopt healthier eating habits, supported by a structured diet and behavioral modification program, played a co-adjuvant role in weight loss and maintenance. The IGB itself, as well as the procedure for its placement, appears to be safe. Despite the limited additional benefit of the IGB in promoting weight loss, its cost-effectiveness should be weighed against the benefits of a comprehensive program focused on dietary and behavioral changes.
